summaries.example: Imagine seeing two dogs. You know they are different animals, but you can also notice that both are dogs. Scotus would say they share a common nature, “dogness,” while each has its own special feature that makes it this particular dog.
summaries.summary: John Duns Scotus was a major medieval thinker who wrote about God, reality, knowledge, and morality. He taught that our knowledge begins with sensible things, but careful thinking can lead us to ideas about God. Scotus gave special importance to the idea of “infinite being”: God has perfection without any limit. He also studied how things can share a nature, such as two people both being human, while each remains a different individual. In his theory of knowledge, the senses give us information and the mind forms general ideas from it. Scotus believed that people can know some truths with certainty through reason, experience, and understanding their own thoughts. He also held that freedom is rooted in the will, which can choose among possibilities at the very moment of choice. The entry also explains his life, his teaching in Oxford, Paris, and Cologne, and the many lecture notes and commentaries connected with his work.
key_ideas: Scotus thought people can use reason and experience to learn some things about God, even without relying only on revelation.
He said some words, such as “good,” can have the same basic meaning when used about God and creatures, though God has goodness without limit.
He described metaphysics as the study of being simply as being.
He believed the mind can gain knowledge from the senses and can also know some truths with certainty.
He argued that genuine freedom belongs especially to the will, our power to choose.
summaries.why_it_matters: Scotus shows how one thinker can connect many questions: What exists? How do we know? What does it mean to choose freely? His ideas help us see that philosophers may agree about some starting points while disagreeing about how language, reason, and faith work together. His careful distinctions also show why a small difference in a word—such as “same” or “different”—can change a whole argument.

important_terms.definition: A philosopher and theologian from the Middle Ages who studied God, knowledge, reality, and human choice.
The study of what is real, what exists, and how different kinds of things are related.
A general feature that can belong to many individual things, such as being a dog or being human.
The process by which the mind gets a general idea from things it senses.
The power to choose between possibilities, including the ability to choose differently at the same moment.

questions_to_think_about: Can we learn important truths by thinking carefully about everyday experience?
What makes two things alike while still being different individuals?
Does being free mean only doing what we want, or must we be able to choose another way?
Can a person be certain about some things? How might we check?

summaries.example: Suppose a student decides whether to help a classmate. The student may understand several reasons for helping, but Scotus would say freedom is not merely the fact that different choices become available at different times. At the instant of choosing one action, the will must have the power to choose otherwise. This is Scotus’s idea of synchronic contingency: alternatives remain genuinely open at the same moment.
summaries.summary: John Duns Scotus was a Franciscan philosopher-theologian whose work shaped medieval debates about natural theology, metaphysics, cognition, and ethics. In natural theology, he argues from experienced effects toward a first agent, a first goal, and a being of maximal excellence. He then argues that these primacies belong together and that the resulting being has intellect, will, and infinity. The concept of infinite being also supports his account of theological language: pure perfections can be predicated univocally of God and creatures, though creatures possess them in limited degrees. In metaphysics, Scotus makes being qua being the subject of the discipline. He develops accounts of matter and form, allows the possibility of prime matter, rejects universal hylomorphism, and defends a plurality of substantial forms in some cases. His theory of universals combines a common nature with a haecceity that individuates it. In epistemology, he explains abstraction from sensory images while also defending intuitive intellectual cognition. Against skepticism and illuminationism, he maintains that natural human powers can achieve certainty in several domains. In ethics, he distinguishes strict natural law, containing necessary truths, from weaker moral requirements that depend on divine will. His account of freedom places its source in the will itself and requires the ability to choose otherwise at the moment of choice.
key_ideas: Scotus’s natural theology begins from effects and creatures, then argues toward a first cause, a first goal, and a maximally excellent being. He calls this a triple primacy.
His concept of “infinite being” is central: infinity is a positive, intrinsic mode of perfection, not merely the absence of a boundary.
Metaphysics studies being as being and includes the study of transcendentals such as being, unity, truth, goodness, and certain disjunctions such as finite-or-infinite.
Scotus is a realist about universals. A common nature is present in individuals, while a haecceity accounts for their individual difference.
Human cognition normally begins with sensation and abstraction, but Scotus also allows intellectual intuitive cognition of present sensible objects and of one’s own mental acts.

Scotus rejects both skepticism and the need for special illumination, arguing that natural intellectual powers can yield certainty in first principles, some causal judgments, certain knowledge of one’s acts, and properly assessed present sensory judgments.
summaries.why_it_matters: Scotus matters because he treats philosophical arguments as interlocking systems. His views about language affect how one can reason about God; his account of infinity supports both his metaphysics and theology; and his theory of the will gives freedom a stronger meaning than merely having different desires over time. His discussions also preserve live philosophical problems: how universals relate to individuals, whether certainty is possible, and how moral necessity differs from divine choice. The SEP entry presents these positions as historically situated arguments, including places where Scotus’s interpretation or the relation among his texts remains debated.

important_terms.definition: Reasoning about God’s existence and attributes without depending on a revealed religious text as its starting point.
Using a predicate with the same basic meaning of God and creatures, rather than using it in wholly different but related senses.
A perfection that involves no limitation or defect, such as goodness or wisdom considered without an upper bound.
The study of being as such, rather than being only as material, living, or belonging to some narrower class.
The feature shared by individuals of a kind, existing outside the mind only in particular things.
Scotus’s term for the principle that makes one individual distinct from other individuals of the same nature.
Knowledge of a particular thing as existing at the present moment, contrasted with knowledge of a general concept.
The capacity of the will to have more than one genuine option at the very moment of choice.

questions_to_think_about: Does applying the word “good” to both creatures and God require one shared concept, or can the meanings merely be related?
Why does Scotus distinguish essentially ordered causes from accidentally ordered causes, and why does that distinction matter to his argument for a first agent?
Can a universal exist outside the mind without being a separate object existing on its own?
What is the difference between knowing what a dog is and knowing that this dog exists right now?
Is a choice fully free if the agent could choose differently only later, rather than at the same moment?

summaries.example: Think about the word “fair.” You might call a class rule fair and also call a person fair. Scotus’s view about God is more demanding: when we call God good, he thinks “good” must connect with the same basic concept used for creatures. The difference is that creatures have goodness in limited ways, while God has it without limit.
summaries.summary: John Duns Scotus was a highly influential thinker of the High Middle Ages. He wrote as both a philosopher and a theologian, and his work covers God, reality, knowledge, and moral choice. Scotus believed that natural theology could begin with sensible creatures and reason toward God. His argument seeks a first agent, a first goal, and a being that is greatest in excellence. He connects these features and argues that the resulting being is intelligent, willing, and infinite. The idea of infinite being is important because Scotus treats infinity as a real, positive perfection rather than merely a lack of limits. This supports his account of univocal language, according to which some concepts, including pure perfections, can apply to God and creatures with the same basic meaning. In metaphysics, he studies being as being. He argues about matter and form, including whether matter can exist without form, and develops a realist account of universals. A common nature can be shared by individuals, while a haecceity makes each individual distinct. In his theory of knowledge, sensation supplies material that the intellect abstracts into general concepts. Scotus also describes intuitive cognition, which concerns a particular thing as existing now. In ethics and psychology, he says some moral truths are necessary, while other moral requirements depend on divine will. He locates freedom in the will and says a free agent must be able to choose otherwise at the moment of choosing.
key_ideas: Scotus thought human reasoning can move from ordinary experience to conclusions about a first cause and the nature of God.
He disagreed with the view that words about God must always have a different but related meaning from the same words about creatures.
He described metaphysics as the study of being itself and examined substance, accidents, matter, form, universals, and individuals.
He explained general ideas through abstraction from sensory experience, while also allowing a special kind of intellectual knowledge of present things.
Scotus opposed skepticism and the claim that special divine illumination is needed for all certainty.
He argued that freedom requires the will to be able to choose differently at the very time it chooses.
summaries.why_it_matters: Scotus is useful for understanding how medieval philosophers combined logical analysis with questions about faith and human life. His distinctions clarify disagreements about religious language, universals, certainty, and free will. They also show that medieval philosophy was not one single viewpoint: Scotus develops positions that differ from thinkers such as Aquinas and Henry of Ghent. Studying him helps readers ask how arguments about reality influence arguments about knowledge, morality, and freedom.

important_terms.definition: The study of God using arguments based on reason and the world, rather than depending on revelation as the argument’s source.
Using a word with the same basic meaning in two cases, even when one case has the feature in a limited way and the other without limit.
A feature that is better to have than not to have in every respect and that does not imply a limitation.
A philosophical discipline concerned with being itself, including what kinds of things exist and how they change.
A nature shared by individuals, such as humanity shared by Socrates and Plato, though it exists outside the mind only in individuals.
The feature that makes one individual of a shared nature different from another individual.
Cognition of a particular thing as existing now, rather than merely understanding its general type.

questions_to_think_about: If two things are both good, must “good” mean the same thing in both cases?
What makes two people both human but still two different people?
How might knowing a general idea differ from knowing that something exists right now?
Can experience and reasoning provide certainty, or do they always leave room for doubt?
Why might freedom require more than having different choices at different times?
